title: When 'computer' was a job title
hook: For 300 years, a computer was a person with a pencil, not a machine.
peek: Long before electronic machines, 'computer' meant a person who did calculations for a living. Teams of human computers worked out comet orbits, star catalogues and rocket paths, and the machines later inherited their job title.
lede: The word computer first appears in English in 1613, meaning someone who computes. For the next three centuries that is all it meant. Astronomers, navigators and engineers hired people to do long calculations by hand, often splitting a big problem into pieces and handing each to a different computer. Only in the 1940s did the word start to mean an electronic machine.

bullets.text: To predict the comet's return, the French mathematician Alexis Clairaut split the work with Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute. They calculated for months, and the comet came back within about a month of their date.

From the 1880s, Harvard College Observatory employed a team of women to measure and classify stars on glass photographs. Among them, Henrietta Leavitt found a key to measuring cosmic distances and Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stars.

At NASA's forerunner, groups of women worked as computers on aircraft and rocket maths. Before John Glenn's 1962 orbit, he reportedly asked for Katherine Johnson to check the electronic computer's numbers by hand.

Early electronic machines were often called automatic computers, to tell them apart from the human kind. As the machines took over the work, the adjective dropped away and the people's job title went with it.
